article.articleHeadline: Kagera heightens Ebola surveillance at borders, schools - Daily News
article.articleSummary: Kagera Region, Tanzania, has intensified Ebola surveillance by mandating school-based screening for all students arriving from neighboring countries with reported Ebola cases, to prevent spread into Tanzania. Regional Health Officer Yassin Mwinori directed eight councils to ensure screening for every incoming student from affected countries. Cross-border measures include thermal screening at Mutukula in Missenyi District and Kabanga in Ngara District, with isolation centers equipped region-wide for rapid detection and response. About 7,000 community health workers have been deployed, and more than 72,000 travelers have been screened. Authorities urged media, religious leaders, and village leaders to bolster public awareness and surveillance at unofficial entry points, and for border venues and entertainment venues to comply with health regulations. article.articleHeadline: Plague - today as dangerous as in the Middle Ages.
article.articleSummary: Plague (Yersinia pestis) remains deadly, with bubonic, septicemic, and pneumonic forms. Bubonic plague is flea-transmitted from infected rodents; septicemic is bloodstream infection; pneumonic spreads via droplets and can pass between people. Global incidence is about 3,000 cases per year, with the DRC, Uganda, and especially Madagascar most affected; Madagascar records roughly 250–500 infections annually and experienced a major outbreak in 2017. Cases also occur in the western United States, including Oregon. Early, nonspecific flu-like symptoms can delay diagnosis; treatment is life-saving. A notable Oregon case involved Paul Gaylord, who contracted plague after a sick cat bite and nearly died, ultimately surviving after ICU care. Evolutionarily, Y. pestis acquired flea transmission (ymt gene) in late Bronze Age, enabling pandemics; Europe largely saw plague disappear by 1945, with Corsica the last locale. Prompt diagnosis and treatment determine outcomes.

article.articleHeadline: Kisangani: Commercial activities continue normally at the central market despite the Ebola alert - ACP.
article.articleSummary: Kisangani, Democratic Republic of the Congo – As of 18 July 2026, commercial activity at Kisangani’s central market in Tshopo province continues normally despite an Ebola virus disease alert. Preventive measures are not visibly implemented: market entrances lack handwashing facilities and awareness messages are sparse. Market manager Franck Lokenge says he has instructed inspectors and staff to intensify sensitization, reminding vendors and buyers of risk-reducing behaviors. Some traders report having heard of Ebola but have not altered their routines, pledging compliance if authorities require measures; buyers suggest stronger awareness campaigns. Authorities hope local outreach will boost vigilance and support the public health response to the Ebola alert, even as health officials monitor the situation.

article.articleHeadline: Walikale: Heavy rains flood several neighborhoods, residents denounce the lack of drainage and fear epidemics.
article.articleSummary: Heavy rains in Walikale rural commune, Nord-Kivu, began around 3:00 am on Friday, July 17, triggering widespread floods in Camp TP, Kisima, Nyalusukula and surrounding areas. Floodwaters entered homes, damaged valuables, and left streets impassable, with residents waking to water at their feet and mud covering interiors. In Camp TP, residents blame nonfunctional drainage for rapid inundation; in Kisima, drainage channels are reportedly blocked by improper waste disposal, worsening floods. In Nyalusukula, runoff carries toilet waste, raising fears of waterborne diseases such as cholera and diarrhea. Kigoma residents call for opening and regular cleaning of canals and linking them to small rivers to improve drainage. Authorities are urged to intervene urgently to upgrade drainage infrastructure and promote sanitation to prevent health risks and future flooding in the context of unplanned urban development.

article.articleHeadline: Inside East Africa's disease highway as cholera cases double across borders
article.articleSummary: Cholera cases across Eastern Africa more than doubled in Q2 2026, rising from about 5,500 to 12,400, while mpox reached 457 cases from January to May 2026. The surge follows the Northern Corridor trade route from Mombasa through Nairobi, Nakuru, Eldoret, Malaba and Busia to Uganda, Rwanda (Kigali), South Sudan (Juba) and eastern DRC, illustrating how transport networks can drive cross-border transmission in displacement- and climate-vulnerable areas. OCHA notes conflict, displacement and climate shocks intensify needs in one of the world’s most severe humanitarian hotspots, with an estimated 48.5 million people requiring aid in 2026 and about 6 million refugees plus 16.7 million internally displaced. Four drivers—expanding trade, displacement, climate shocks and underfunded surveillance—shape risk. Border points Malaba, Busia, Namanga and Elegu are key for monitoring; stronger surveillance, lab networks and real-time outbreak monitoring are urged as climate patterns raise cholera risk through September and potential floods later in the year.

article.articleHeadline: Septic shock due to a splenic abscess.
article.articleSummary: Septic shock from a splenic abscess in a 70-year-old woman, treated after presentation in Cambodia and evacuation to Vietnam. A large splenic abscess ruptured, causing pleural effusion and left lung collapse; she developed septic shock and multi-organ dysfunction, requiring ICU care. Emergency splenectomy with intra-abdominal debridement was performed at Gia An 115 Hospital (Vietnam) after transfer on 17 July; nearly three weeks of intensive care led to stabilization and discharge. Splenic abscesses pose high mortality risk due to compromised immunity and risk of bacteremia; infection can spread and trigger septic shock if not treated promptly. Initial symptoms are nonspecific—prolonged fever, dull abdominal pain, fatigue, weight loss—often delaying diagnosis. Clinicians urge prompt evaluation for persistent fever of unknown origin, abdominal pain, fatigue, weight loss, or dyspnea, as progression to bacteremia or septic shock markedly increases mortality.

article.articleHeadline: Dien Bien Province Focuses on Containing the Lumpy Skin Disease Outbreak in Cattle
article.articleSummary: As of July 18, 2026, Dien Bien Province reports a lumpy skin disease outbreak in cattle centered in Sam Mứn commune (Ca Hâu) and Núa Ngam commune (Na Tông, Hin Phon, Tân Quang), Vietnam. The first outbreak was detected May 28 at household Vừ A Tú, Ca Hâu, with 38 cattle across 13 households ill and 2 deaths, followed by cases in Co Cang and Púng Bửa. In Núa Ngam, 21 cattle across 15 households in Na Tông, Hin Phon, Tân Quang also contracted. Laboratory confirmation by the Central Veterinary Diagnostic and Testing Center I identified lumpy skin disease virus in samples from Sam Mứn and Núa Ngam. All affected cattle have been treated per protocol and recovered; no new outbreaks have arisen. Ongoing risks include waning vaccine immunity, free grazing, high animal movement, and vectors; authorities urge strict, early detection, localized containment and disinfection to prevent spread.

article.articleHeadline: Child with seizures and cyanosis due to EV71 hand-foot-mouth disease, even without fever.
article.articleSummary: On July 9, a previously healthy child in Vietnam developed seizures and cyanosis during a trip, with no fever. A provincial hospital initially diagnosed pneumonia; at National Children’s Hospital, tests showed elevated white blood cells and Enterovirus 71 (EV71) positivity, with bronchitis, pneumonia, and mild otitis media. The child recovered from the acute episode but remains under treatment and monitoring. EV71 is a major cause of hand-foot-mouth disease and can cause severe CNS complications—seizures, meningitis, encephalitis—even without fever. Parents are warned not to ignore abnormal signs and to seek urgent pediatric care. Seizure first aid includes lying the child on a flat surface on their side, not restraining limbs, not placing objects in the mouth, and seeking emergency care after the episode; blood tests and PCR help confirm EV71 infection.

article.articleHeadline: Dak Lak takes proactive measures to address the risk of a new virus in livestock.
article.articleSummary: On July 17, 2026, Dak Lak Province launched 2026 action plans to prevent and control terrestrial animal diseases, focusing on ASF, rabies, and emerging viral threats. Since January, ASF outbreaks have affected 113 households in 30 communes/wards, leading to the culling of more than 8,500 pigs (over 440 tons). Two communes, Krông Năng and Hòa Phú, have not yet passed 21 days since their outbreak. Rabies outbreaks reached 11 in 10 communes, with 24 dogs/cats culled; vaccination coverage for rabies is 28.3%. Surveillance detected an ASF virus genotype I–II recombinant in Dak Lak, a strain not protected by vaccines, and the exotic foot-and-mouth disease serotype SAT1, first seen in China, raises import risk. Authorities called for early detection, strict control of farming, slaughter, and transport, disease-free zones, better dog/cat management, and expanded vaccination, supported by an enhanced animal disease information system; leadership accountability at the commune/ward level was emphasized.

article.articleHeadline: Parasites on raw vegetables: how to eat safely?
article.articleSummary: Cyclosporiasis, a diarrheal illness caused by Cyclospora cayetanensis, is linked to raw vegetables. The US CDC reports thousands of cases across many states, with hundreds linked to a single contaminated source; leafy greens are under surveillance. Cyclospora contaminates produce via irrigation water, soil, harvest, or handling, causing watery diarrhea, abdominal pain, bloating, nausea, fatigue, and weight loss; fever is usually mild. Children, the elderly, and immunocompromised individuals face higher dehydration and hospitalization risk. In Vietnam, where many dishes include raw herbs, washing under running water (sometimes with vinegar) is advised, though not foolproof; heating to 72°C or higher reduces risk. No confirmed cyclosporiasis cases in Vietnam yet, but precautions are advised. Separately, in Gia Lai province, dozens developed abdominal pain and diarrhea after eating bread at a shop on Hung Vuong Street, Quy Nhơn Ward, and were hospitalized.

article.articleHeadline: Virus killer, surveillance remains high. "West Nile virus, infections even without symptoms. But small precautions are enough."
article.articleSummary: As of 18 July 2026, Italy reports elevated arbovirus activity: in Emilia-Romagna an elderly person infected with West Nile virus in Modena, and West Nile–positive mosquitoes detected in six provinces; Marche maintains very high surveillance with no human cases. Warmer-than-average temperatures heighten arbovirus risk. West Nile virus infections are mostly asymptomatic; West Nile encephalitis accounts for about 1% of cases with high mortality in those with comorbidities. Dengue, transmitted by the tiger mosquito (Aedes aegypti), has appeared in Marche and Emilia-Romagna in prior years; symptoms are typically fever for a few days, though infection with a different serotype can trigger hemorrhagic illness. Prevention relies on vector control and practical measures to avoid standing water; a vaccine exists and is recommended for people who have already contracted the virus traveling to risk areas such as India. Ebola remains unlikely in Europe despite Africa-endemic transmission, but strict isolation protocols apply and there is no widely available commercial vaccine.

Demands include an intensive drive to eliminate water contamination, improved sanitation, a dedicated diarrhoea treatment ward in a government hospital, and reimbursement of medical expenses for patients treated in private hospitals. Background notes more than 15 people have died in Vijayawada from diarrhoea and gastroenteritis outbreaks in the past two years, including Moghalrajpuram and New Rajarajeswari Peta. With COVID-19 cases in the state, public health priorities and safe drinking water across Vijayawada are urged.

article.articleHeadline: ICMR's i-DRONE Project In Telangana Boosts TB Testing And Cuts Patient Costs
article.articleSummary: TB in India via ICMR's i-DRONE (Drone-based Medical Delivery Initiative) pilot in Yadadri-Bhuvanagiri district, India. The hub-and-spoke network connects 11 Primary Health Centres, 60 sub-centres and four TB Units to diagnostic laboratories, using drones to transport sputum samples and to deliver anti-TB medicines, strengthening last-mile care. The 840-participant study observed median time to TB diagnosis drop from 15 days to 5 days, enabling earlier treatment and reducing transmission risk. Drones supplement healthcare workers, not replace them. This approach demonstrates faster sample transport and medicine delivery in rural settings, with potential for broader rollout across India's TB-control efforts.

article.articleHeadline: CG News: Trial successful in Surguja; indigenous African Swine Fever vaccine launched in Delhi, a major achievement for the country in the field of veterinary medicine.
article.articleSummary: India has achieved a historic veterinary milestone as scientists at the National Institute of High Security Animal Diseases (NIHSAD), Bhopal, developed a domestically produced African Swine Fever (ASF) vaccine. The MA-104 cell-based live-attenuated vaccine is the world’s first of its kind and can be produced at scale on a commercially available cell line, enabling low-cost manufacturing. Field trials began March 2026 at Sukar Farm Sakalo in Ambikapur, Surguja district, Chhattisgarh, under supervision of NIHSAD experts Raju Kumar, Sainthil, Venkatesh, and Fateh Singh; initial results show safety and immunogenicity were fully satisfactory. A 1 ml intramuscular dose is given, with a booster after 14 days; healthy pigs eight weeks and older developed robust immunity for up to six months, with no risk of reversion to virulence. Minister Shivraj Singh Chouhan presented the vaccine in New Delhi during ICAR’s 98th Foundation Day.

article.articleHeadline: WHO India Records Over 26,000 Measles Cases In 12 Months: How Long Does The Vaccine Keeps You Safe?
article.articleSummary: India reported 26,627 measles cases in 12 months, the second-highest burden according to WHO data. The rise highlights gaps in vaccination and surveillance amid outbreaks. Measles is contagious and spreads via respiratory droplets; an infected person can transmit to up to 90% of unvaccinated close contacts, with the virus lingering in the air for up to two hours. Symptoms typically appear 10–14 days after exposure and start with high fever, cough, runny nose, and red eyes, followed by a red blotchy rash; Koplik spots may precede the rash. Two doses of measles-containing vaccine offer long-lasting protection, with one dose providing roughly 93–95%. In India, the MR vaccine is given in two doses at 9–12 months and 16–24 months. Most adults with two childhood doses need no booster; exceptions apply for unclear records or high-risk groups. Seek care for fever with rash or respiratory symptoms, especially in infants under 1 year.

article.articleHeadline: Climate change may reverse decades of progress against waterborne diseases, new study finds
article.articleSummary: New Delhi, 18 July 2026 — A global review in Nature Reviews Microbiology warns climate change could reverse decades of gains against waterborne diseases, threatening cholera, diarrhoea and other infections in vulnerable communities with limited water and sanitation. Rising temperatures, floods and droughts alter environmental conditions that govern pathogen survival, replication and virulence, potentially increasing outbreaks in both urban and rural settings. Drought reduces safe water access and concentrates microbes, while floods overwhelm sanitation systems and spread contamination. Pathogen responses vary: higher temperatures generally boost many bacteria and protozoa; some viruses (norovirus, rotavirus, adenovirus) spread more efficiently in cooler, drier conditions. The burden remains greatest in low- and middle-income countries, with diarrhoeal diseases causing about 1.2 million deaths annually, disproportionately affecting children under five. Calls for disease-specific public health strategies to counter climate-driven shifts.

article.articleHeadline: Lull in monsoon leads to mosquito menace in city
article.articleSummary: A lull in the monsoon and higher daytime temperatures have sparked a mosquito surge in Nagpur. June monitoring shows vulnerabilities, with Mangalwari Zone recording the highest Culex and Aedes counts, vectors for filariasis, dengue, and chikungunya; Gandhibagh is the only zone with Anopheles, which transmit malaria. Dense populations, poor drainage, junkyards, and water-logging are major breeding spots, including Patankar Chowk, Uppalwadi, Yashodharanagar, Mankapur, Zingabai Takli, Khamla, Sonegaon, Gittikhadan, Mominpura, and Kalamna. In response, Nagpur Municipal Corporation deploys a multi-layer containment grid: mechanised fogging (vehicle-mounted, portable and cold foggers, high-pressure pump sprayers) and targeted larvicides (mosquito larvicidal oil and emulsified oils) in open drains and stagnant water. Rapid Response Teams act on lab-confirmed dengue or malaria, conducting surveillance testing and spatial fogging within a 25-house radius. Public participation is urged—weekly checks for standing water, use of BTI and larvicidal tablets, and ongoing structural inspections during monsoon.

article.articleHeadline: Mario Lugones reviewed the week's main advances: AI, medications, and dengue prevention.

article.articleHeadline: Include these Vitamin C-rich foods in your diet to reduce viral infections.
article.articleSummary: Monsoon humidity boosts bacterial and viral infections such as cold, cough, flu, and stomach upset. Include citrus fruits—lemon, orange, mosambi (sweet lime), and chakotra (grapefruit)—and consider a morning lemon water or a daily orange. Amla (Indian gooseberry) is described as a superfood with about 20 times more Vitamin C than other sour fruits and aids detoxification. Guava contains more Vitamin C than orange and provides dietary fiber to ease digestion. Kiwi is a compact source of Vitamin C, and red bell peppers have very high Vitamin C. Together, these foods may bolster immunity and digestion during the monsoon.

article.articleHeadline: This is what the little-known tick-borne virus is like: in some cases it can be severe and even fatal.
article.articleSummary: Tick-borne Orthonairovirus is a lesser-known group that can cause severe illness beyond Lyme disease. The best-known member is Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever virus, with a fatality rate of about 10–40% among severe cases. Orthonairovirus has a three-segment RNA genome, enabling genetic reassortment. Other members include Yezo virus in Japan and Antu virus in China. Transmission is mainly through tick bites, but can also occur via contact with blood of an ill animal or bodily fluids of an infected person. Early symptoms typically include very high fever and malaise, progressing rapidly. Prevention focuses on avoiding tick bites: wear light clothing, cover skin with long sleeves and pants, use DEET on exposed skin or permethrin on clothing, and perform thorough checks for ticks after outdoor activities.

article.articleHeadline: Guangdong Man's Cow Dies After Eating a Stick Insect; Isn't the Stick Insect Non-Toxic? Netizens: I've Heard This From Older Folks—Never Thought It Could Be True!
article.articleSummary: Guangdong, China: a Lei Zhou Yellow cow reportedly died after eating a stick insect, fueling online claims that stick insects are toxic. Folk beliefs about cows dying after eating stick insects are widespread in Fujian, Guangdong, Guangxi and Guizhou, but experts say Guangdong's local stick insects are not known to be poisonous. The more plausible cause is infection with iron-worm larvae (铁线虫) carried by some stick insects from contaminated water or plants. Eggs in water can contaminate insects; cattle ingest infected insects, allowing larvae to invade the digestive tract and damage bile ducts and intestinal walls, causing severe gas production in the rumen, excessive drinking, foaming at the mouth, and impaired balance. Severe cases may perforate organs or cause suffocation; illness can last days to weeks. Treatment exists via veterinary puncture to relieve gas and deworming. This case highlights information gaps and the persistence of folk beliefs without scientific confirmation.

article.articleHeadline: Even after being left out for four hours, cooked foods should be reheated thoroughly before eating! Summer sees a high incidence of infectious diarrhea, and experts offer these reminders.
article.articleSummary: Cholera and bacterial dysentery risk rises in Jiangsu Province, China, amid hot summer, as high temperatures accelerate food spoilage and pathogen growth. Dr. Zhu Liguo of Jiangsu CDC notes abdominal pain, diarrhea, nausea, vomiting, with fever in some cases; patients and carriers are the main sources, transmission via direct contact with feces or contaminated surfaces, and through contaminated food or water. Common foodborne sources include shellfish and inadequately washed produce. Preventive measures emphasize hand hygiene (soap and water for at least 20 seconds) after restroom use, before meals, and after handling waste or animals; avoid swimming during diarrhea; separate raw and cooked foods; cook meat and eggs thoroughly; wash produce; avoid spoiled or dead animals. Do not keep cooked foods beyond four hours; reheat thoroughly before eating; drink boiled or certified safe water. Seek medical care for diarrhea/vomiting and isolate at home; food workers should stop handling food if symptomatic and follow disinfection protocols.

article.articleHeadline: Metatranscriptomics reveals urbanization-driven divergence in rodent viromes and zoonotic risks in Chinese megacities
article.articleSummary: 1,072 rodents from Wuhan and Shenzhen, two Chinese megacities, across four species yielded 35 vertebrate-associated viruses by metagenomic sequencing. Nine are potentially novel, including Norovirus and Orthopicobirnavirus; three have zoonotic potential: Orthohantavirus Seoulense and human coronavirus OC43 (HCoV_OC43). Two viruses previously unreported in rodents—Erinaceus hedgehog Seoul orthohantavirus and Canine astrovirus—reveal cross-order transmission risk. Twenty-two viruses were classified as high-risk, with Wuhan and Shenzhen showing distinct prevalence patterns. Inter-city rectal virome divergence is structured by meteorological variables and independently explains about 5% of variation in viral community composition, underscoring the role of spatial distance in distribution and transmission of rodent-borne viruses. Implications: proactive surveillance and mitigation of emerging zoonotic threats in dense urban environments.

article.articleHeadline: Diagnosing Pulmonary Embolism in Cancer Patients; Infections in U.S. Hospitals
article.articleSummary: Healthcare-associated infections (HAIs) in U.S. hospitals declined in 2023 versus 2015. A New England Journal of Medicine Emerging Infections Program survey of roughly 14,000 patients across 218 hospitals found 2.6% had at least one HAI in 2023, down from 3.2% in 2015, with about 60% not device-associated. The fall is largely driven by fewer Clostridioides difficile infections due to enhanced testing, antimicrobial stewardship, and infection control, along with reductions in central-line–associated bloodstream infections (CLABSI) and catheter-associated urinary tract infections (CAUTI). MRSA comprised about 46% of Staphylococcus infections, while other pathogens are emerging. TTHealthWatch also discusses diagnosing pulmonary embolism in cancer patients via an emergency department algorithm that performs well, amyloid clearance in Alzheimer's showing region-specific responses to new agents, and a China-based trial evaluating extending dual antiplatelet therapy after multivessel stenting, weighing bleeding risk.

article.articleSummary: Shanghai, China—A 26-year-old fitness trainer was diagnosed with HIV/AIDS after a routine infectious-disease screen, illustrating how early clues are often misread as workout fatigue. Eight months before diagnosis she had three alarms: afternoon persistent low-grade fever (37.5–37.8°C); progressive fatigue with core weakness, reduced grip strength, and rapid heart rate during lifts; a painless white tongue lesion later identified as oral candidiasis. Routine testing during license renewal yielded a positive HIV antibody; CD4 count had fallen below 350 cells/μL, prompting immediate antiretroviral therapy. The piece stresses urgent post-exposure prophylaxis within 72 hours of exposure; beyond this window, a fourth-week HIV antigen/antibody test detects over 95% of infections. Warning signs—oral thrush, painless lymphadenopathy, recurrent shingles—should trigger infectious-disease consultation. ART is lifelong; side effects may include lipodystrophy, reduced bone density, and cardiovascular risk. The patient remains on ART with viral load suppressed.

article.articleHeadline: A novel influenza strain has emerged in Hong Kong, spreading alarmingly... Could it trigger a pandemic?
article.articleSummary: Influenza strain known as the Hong Kong flu (Influenza A) has re-emerged in Asia, with rising respiratory infections in parts of Asia and increased travel to destinations such as Hong Kong and Bali, Indonesia. Russian virologist Victoria Cherbakova notes the situation signals heightened activity typical of seasonal influenza A rather than a new pandemic. Dense travel and gatherings in tourist areas, coupled with weather changes, may boost transmission, and some respiratory viruses can briefly persist on surfaces, underscoring the need for hygiene and disinfection. Transmission occurs via droplets and airborne routes, especially in closed, crowded spaces; improving ventilation and avoiding close contact when symptomatic is advised. Early treatment after symptom onset can shorten illness and limit viral replication, with medications used under medical supervision. Hydration, rest, fever control, and avoiding exertion until full recovery. Ongoing travel and public health measures remain crucial to limiting seasonal influenza and its complications.

article.articleHeadline: 208 Bhabinkamtibmas Deployed to Track TB Cases in Sragen
article.articleSummary: 208 Bhabinkamtibmas police community liaison officers were deployed across Sragen Regency, Indonesia, to accelerate tuberculosis (TB) elimination. article.articleSummary: Indonesia faces growing health risks from climate change, with tuberculosis (TB) control among those affected. The CARES program, Climate Action for Resilient and Empowered Healthcare Staff, developed by KUMPUL Impact with AVPN support, strengthens health workers and community cadres to address climate-TB intersections. The initiative kicked off on 21 October 2025, bringing academics, health practitioners, civil society, and communities to explore links between climate and health-system resilience. Prof. Budi Haryanto of University of Indonesia notes climate impacts on health are evident and may rise, potentially increasing TB risks and worsening non-communicable diseases, food security, mental health, and socioeconomic conditions. TB patients may face interrupted treatment and higher household costs during climate events. CARES developed Climate-TB training modules and delivered webinars via Plataran Sehat, with cadre training alongside PPTI Pusat, covering vulnerable groups, transmission, and health-service access challenges. Policy integration, research gaps, and cross-sector collaboration remain priorities.

article.articleHeadline: HIV Case Findings in Pringsewu Increase, Health Office Says Screening Is Expanding.
article.articleSummary: Pringsewu Regency Health Office reports higher HIV case findings in the first half of 2026 compared with 2025, attributing the rise to expanded screening and active case finding rather than necessarily increased transmission. By mid-2026, 432 people living with HIV are on antiretroviral therapy across Pringsewu. The majority of cases remain among the productive age group 25–49, with higher detection in districts with larger populations and better health-service access. Risk factors include unprotected sexual activity (heterosexual and key populations), spousal transmission, and mother-to-child transmission, prompting continued antenatal HIV screening. Testing is expanding at all puskesmas and hospitals, prioritizing pregnant women, TB, sexually transmitted infections, hepatitis, and at-risk groups, including outreach with puskesmas and peer supporters. Adherence is generally good, but some patients discontinue treatment; stigma and fear hinder early detection. ARV stock is secure; shortages would be coordinated with Lampung Provincial Health Office and the Ministry of Health.

article.articleHeadline: Dr Panda Lab warns: Students found bringing tattoo equipment to school to tattoo each other, risking infection.
article.articleSummary: Dr Panda Lab warns on Facebook that some students have brought tattoo equipment to schools to tattoo each other, with details about any specific school not yet confirmed. The page notes that schools are not sterile environments; tattooing in classrooms or bathrooms could expose wounds to dust and bacteria, increasing the risk of skin infection, inflammation, or abscess. It also flags the danger of blood-borne infections if the tattooist lacks hygiene knowledge, reuses needles, or uses non-standard equipment, potentially spreading hepatitis B, hepatitis C, and HIV. The advisory urges parents to be alert for such activities as of 2026-07-18. No incidents confirmed at any particular school yet.

article.articleHeadline: Federal District steps up the fight against dengue ahead of the rainy season.
article.articleSummary: Dengue remains a public health priority in the Federal District (Brasília) as of 2026-07-18, with prevention emphasized ahead of the rainy season. After a peak in 2024 (over 277,000 probable dengue cases and nearly 7,000 hospitalizations), DF reported 10,671 cases in 2025 and 3,754 in 2026 to date, driven by the Aedes aegypti vector. The primary strategy is eliminating breeding sites during the dry season and environmental education, not punitive actions. Inspections in Asa Norte highlighted ongoing risks from water in plant saucers; authorities stress chlorine as essential for disinfection, noting household bleach is less effective. Vaccination is available for children and adolescents aged 10–14. Residents in Varjão and Fercal described routine measures to avoid standing water, such as draining plant pots and reusing laundry water. Notable risk spots included an abandoned pool and tires stored improperly that collected water.

article.articleHeadline: Dengue, Zika, Chikungunya: invasive mosquitoes cost billions, prevention lags behind.
article.articleSummary: From 1975 to 2020, costs linked to invasive Aedes mosquitoes and the diseases they transmit—dengue, chikungunya, and Zika—total at least $94.7 billion (in 2022 dollars), with higher estimates over $300 billion when long-term sequelae are included. Dengue alone accounts for about 80% of costs. Annual costs exceed $3 billion on average, with a peak above $20 billion in 2013. Costs cover medical care, productivity losses, and public expenditure for surveillance and vector control, plus indirect impacts like absenteeism. The global spread of Aedes aegypti (originating in Africa, now in tropical/subtropical Americas, Asia, and Oceania) and Aedes albopictus (the tiger mosquito, spreading worldwide since the 1970s) has fueled more epidemics across Europe, North America, and the Americas. In 2023–2024 Latin American countries such as Brazil and Argentina experienced historic multi‑million case outbreaks. Prevention spending is about ten times lower than response costs, and estimates are likely conservative.

triage.triage_reason: 本記事は1975年〜2020年の蚊媒介感染症の経済的コストに関する分析・総説記事であり、新規または進行中の具体的な感染症発生シグナルではないため、トリアージ対象外と判断する。

article.articleHeadline: For the first time: an Argentine company will send foot-and-mouth disease vaccines to an EU country due to a health emergency.
article.articleSummary: Foot-and-mouth disease (FMD) vaccine shipments from Argentina’s Biogénesis Bagó to Cyprus mark the first time an EU member state receives Argentine-made FMD vaccine. About one million doses will be dispatched after Cyprus, in February, lost its FMD-free-without-vaccination status following three Larnaca outbreaks. The circulating serotype is SAT1, of southern Africa origin, now also detected in Lesbos, Israel, and Turkey. Cyprus has imposed animal-movement restrictions, suspended cattle exports, and begun emergency vaccination. The EU prohibited routine vaccination, but allows emergency use. Biogénesis Bagó’s vaccine carries EuFMD precertification from FAO, enabling deployment without local registration. The company also runs national antigen banks (Argentina since 2000; US/Canada since 2006) and supplies Korea, Taiwan, Philippines, and Israel; Brazil has a 10-year antigen bank contract for 10 million doses. Garín plant capacity ~400 million doses/year; ~200 million produced now, with three-quarters exported.

article.articleHeadline: Bat tests positive for rabies, and Betim conducts a vaccination drive.
article.articleSummary: Rabies confirmed in Betim, Brazil, after a bat tested positive in Alterosas - 1ª Seção. The positive result was confirmed on July 15, one day after the animal was found dead in the mouth of a pet dog on Silves Street. The dog had direct contact with the infected bat; zoonoses surveillance recommended euthanasia per the Ministry of Health, but the owner declined. The dog will remain under strict 180-day isolation with no contact with people or other animals, under supervision. To prevent spread, Betim will implement a 500-meter vaccination block around the discovery site, vaccinating dogs and cats from 8:00 to 12:00 on Saturday, July 18, with ongoing operations next week from 8:00 to 17:00 door-to-door. Betim has 1,925 doses of animal rabies vaccine available for immediate use. The vaccination area includes streets Mal-Me-Quer, Melindre, Rondantas, Silves, and nearby avenues.

article.articleHeadline: Weekly Health Update | Ebola Toll Nears 800; Cholera Hits Lake Chad
article.articleSummary: Bundibugy o Ebola in the Democratic Republic of Congo has reached 2,273 cases and 796 deaths, the third-largest outbreak on record, with >80% of new infections occurring outside known contact lists and a Bunia treatment center attacked on July 15. Funding gaps exceed $400 million as WHO and Africa CDC expand beds (>800) and laboratories (16), while UNICEF reports only 25% of requested funds secured. In Uganda, the last patient recovered and a 42-day observation period began July 16; 20 cases and 2 deaths since May 15, with 15 imports from DRC; 836 contacts monitored. Acute diarrhea in Mulungu, Shabunda, South Kivu reports 52 cases and 11 deaths between June 23 and July 7, linked to untreated river water Lubila and Ulindi. Separately, Cameroon and Chad report cholera outbreaks; Nigeria notes rising Lassa fever. West Africa hosts Rift Valley fever coordination in Dakar using DST-FVR.

article.articleHeadline: Teresina records a drop of more than 80% in respiratory virus cases in the first half of 2026.
article.articleSummary: RSV circulation in Teresina, Brazil, fell more than 80% in the first half of 2026, with 39 positive cases confirmed by the Central Laboratory (Lacen), down from 208 in Jan–Jun 2025 (≈81.3% decrease). RSV-associated Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome (SRAG) cases declined to 19 in H1 2026 from 100 in H1 2025 (≈81% decrease). Over half of 2026 cases involved infants under one year. The decline is attributed to maternal vaccination against RSV, added to the National Vaccination Schedule in December 2025, and 80.49% coverage in Teresina, exceeding the 80% target, offering indirect protection to newborns in the first six months. Additionally, February 2026 saw the introduction of nirsevimab in the municipal health network for premature infants (up to 36 weeks+6 days) and certain young children with comorbidities, via SUS. The simultaneous reductions in positive tests and SRAG notifications suggest lower viral circulation and clinical impact, influenced by vaccination and prevention measures.

article.articleHeadline: Foz do Iguaçu Health Department wins national award with dengue and arboviral disease surveillance system
article.articleSummary: Foz do Iguaçu's Municipal Health Department won a national award for its Precision Active Surveillance System for Arboviral Diseases, including dengue surveillance. Recognized as the Best Successful Experience in the South of Brazil at the 21st Mostra Brasil, Aqui Tem SUS, the achievement was announced during the 39th Congresso Nacional do Conasems in Porto Alegre. The system had previously been named the Best Experience of Paraná's 9th Regional Health, securing its national presentation. The Congress brings together municipal and state secretaries and Ministry of Health representatives to discuss SUS policies and innovations. Renata Defante Lopes, coordinator at the Center for Zoonoses Control, said the recognition reinforces investment in health surveillance innovation and demonstrates that municipal experiences can transform public health across the country.

article.articleHeadline: Six brigades traverse Totoracocha to complete vaccination after detecting a suspected measles case in Cuenca.

article.articleHeadline: Measles: New Cases in Brazil Reinforce the Importance of Vaccination.
article.articleSummary: Measles outbreaks in Brazil prompt renewed vaccination emphasis, eight cases this year (seven in São Paulo, one in Rio de Janeiro). Authorities warn that falling vaccination coverage increases susceptibility and the risk of sustained transmission. No antiviral therapy exists; care is supportive. Measles is highly contagious, spreading via droplets; an infected person can transmit to roughly 90% of susceptible close contacts from six days before to four days after rash onset, with initial symptoms such as high fever, cough, coryza, and conjunctivitis. Complications include pneumonia, otitis media, encephalitis (~1 in 1,000), ocular damage, and rare PEESA. Brazil eliminated measles in 2016, lost it in 2019, and regained it in 2024. Vaccines include MMR and tetra-viral; first dose at 12 months, second at 15 months; two-dose coverage advised for ages 5–29 without documented vaccination.

article.articleHeadline: Bird flu could wipe out half of Hawke's Bay gannet colony, sanctuary warns
article.articleSummary: Avian influenza H5N1 has arrived in New Zealand, threatening Hawke’s Bay’s Cape Sanctuary and its seabird colonies. After June’s Australia-origin case, DoC vaccinated critically endangered species at Cape Sanctuary, including 18 takahē; about 1,000 kiwi there are at medium risk and unvaccinated. Stage two confirmed NZ cases: a brown skua found at Petone Beach, Wellington, and a swap harrier hawk/kāhu in Wairarapa. The detections mark the virus’s entry into NZ and underline risk to seabirds, shorebirds, and waterfowl. Stage three would be triggered if a case is found in Hawke’s Bay, prompting partial programme withdrawals to protect human health. Cape Kidnappers’ gannet colony numbers about 20,000–25,000. Northern Hemisphere outbreaks wiped up to 50% of affected gannet colonies; Australasian gannets may be less affected but precautions remain. Gannets are due back from Australia within weeks; the public should report sick/dead birds to MPI 0800 80 99 66 and not touch them.

article.articleHeadline: HOY Daily | Dengue remains at low transmission levels and no hospitalizations or deaths have been reported.
article.articleSummary: Paraguay: Dengue remains at low transmission with a stable trend per the General Directorate of Health Surveillance. Nationwide weekly suspected dengue: 102. In weeks 25–27, only three confirmations: two in Central Department and one in Presidente Hayes; DENV-1 serotype identified. Accumulated 2026 confirmed dengue cases: 288. No hospitalizations or deaths during the period. The Limpio municipality outbreak shows a favorable evolution with decreasing notifications and one confirmed case in recent weeks. Vigilance notes rising suspected case notifications in Asunción and in Central, Presidente Hayes, Alto Paraná, Guairá, Caazapá, Concepción, Itapúa, Cordillera, Misiones, and San Pedro Departments. Chikungunya: year-to-date 18 confirmed cases, three imported from Bolivia. Authorities stress eliminating mosquito breeding sites and seeking timely care for fever, headache, or body pains, and avoiding self-medication. Published July 18, 2026.
